faq.a: MCV tells you the cells are large but not why; you need folate, B12, liver, thyroid, and drug history to pinpoint the aetiology.
faq.q: Why is MCV alone not enough to diagnose the cause?

faq.a: Indirectly, through severe anaemia and folate depletion from repeated haemolysis; treat malaria and replace folate.
In newborns and during pregnancy MCV can be mildly elevated, but values above 100 fL in adults always warrant investigation.
faq.q: Is a high MCV ever normal?

exam: A 35‑year‑old man with HIV on zidovudine presents with fatigue and MCV = 112 fL. – Identify the most likely cause and the next step in management.
A pregnant woman in a rural clinic has Hb = 9 g/dL, MCV = 105 fL, and glossitis. – What deficiency should you treat first and why?
A patient with chronic alcohol use has macrocytosis but normal folate and B12 levels. – Explain the pathophysiology and the appropriate intervention.
You receive a CBC showing MCV = 108 fL and Hb = 7 g/dL in a malaria‑endemic area. – List three investigations you would order and the rationale for each.
A 60‑year‑old farmer presents with macrocytic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy. – Differentiate vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency clinically and biochemically.
During a ward round you see a smear with macro‑ovalocytes and occasional hypersegmented neutrophils. – What does this pattern suggest and what is the urgent complication to watch for?
A patient on carbamazepine develops macrocytosis. – Discuss why this drug causes macrocytosis and how you would manage it.
You suspect myelodysplastic syndrome in an elderly patient with macrocytosis and pancytopenia. – What bone‑marrow finding confirms the diagnosis and why is early referral important?
ai.title: Macrocytic Anemia
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Macrocytic anemia is defined by an increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL). It results from impaired DNA synthesis or altered red cell membrane, leading to large, often oval red cells. Common in low‑resource settings are nutritional deficiencies, alcohol, drugs, and chronic infections.

b: MCV > 100 fL on CBC
Hemoglobin below reference range
Peripheral smear with macro‑ovalocytes
sections.p: Macrocytic anemia is diagnosed when the automated CBC shows MCV greater than 100 fL and the hemoglobin is low for age and sex. A peripheral smear shows large, often oval red cells.

t.b: Confirms anemia and quantifies MCV; a high MCV establishes macrocytosis
Identifies macro‑ovalocytes and excludes schistocytes or sickle cells

b: Mild: Hb 10‑12 g/dL, asymptomatic
Moderate: Hb 8‑9.9 g/dL, fatigue, mild dyspnoea
Severe: Hb < 8 g/dL, tachycardia, dyspnoea at rest
sections.p: Severity is graded by hemoglobin level and clinical impact rather than by MCV alone.

b: Folate deficiency – poor diet, malabsorption, pregnancy
Vitamin B12 deficiency – pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, strict vegetarian diet
Alcohol excess – direct marrow toxicity, folate loss
Antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine) and other marrow‑suppressive drugs
Chronic infections (HIV, TB, malaria) – marrow infiltration or drug side‑effects
Hypothyroidism – reduced erythropoiesis
Myelodysplastic syndrome – especially in older patients
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most frequent causes are nutritional deficiencies, alcohol excess, and drugs, followed by chronic infections and marrow disorders.

b: Fatigue, weakness, pallor
Dyspnoea on exertion
Glossitis or angular cheilitis in folate/B12 deficiency
Peripheral neuropathy in B12 deficiency
History of alcohol use, malnutrition, or drug exposure
sections.p: Patients usually present with symptoms of anaemia and may have additional clues pointing to a specific cause.
Targeted tests identify the underlying aetiology while confirming macrocytosis.

t.b: Is folate deficiency present? Low folate confirms nutritional cause
Is B12 deficiency present? Low B12 points to pernicious anaemia or malabsorption
Detect alcoholic liver disease or cholestasis that can cause macrocytosis
Identify hypothyroidism as a reversible cause
Detect HIV infection that may cause marrow suppression or drug‑related macrocytosis
Distinguish myelodysplastic syndrome from other causes when peripheral work‑up is inconclusive
Assess marrow response; low retic suggests production problem

b: Severe anaemia (Hb < 8 g/dL) with cardiovascular compromise
Neurological deficits (paresthesia, gait disturbance) suggesting B12 deficiency
Unexplained fever or weight loss indicating marrow infiltration
Alcohol‑related macrocytosis – abstinence, nutritional rehabilitation, folate supplementation
Drug‑induced (e.g., zidovudine) – switch to alternative antiretroviral if possible; avoid abrupt withdrawal
Hypothyroidism – levothyroxine replacement; corrects macrocytosis by restoring erythropoiesis
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.

b: Repeat CBC after 2‑4 weeks of therapy; expect MCV to fall toward normal
Re‑check folate/B12 levels after treatment to confirm correction
Educate on balanced diet rich in leafy greens, legumes, and animal protein where culturally acceptable
Screen pregnant women for folate deficiency early
sections.p: Monitor response and address preventable risk factors.

b: Megaloblastic anaemia (subset of macrocytosis due to DNA synthesis defect)
Reticulocytosis – raised MCV from large reticulocytes, not true macrocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis – normocytic or mildly macrocytic but with spherocytes
sections.p: Macrocytic anaemia can be mistaken for other red‑cell size abnormalities.

b: Mixed iron deficiency and folate deficiency can produce a normal MCV despite macrocytosis
Severe dehydration concentrates blood, artificially raising MCV
Automated counters may misclassify macro‑ovalocytes as artefacts; smear review is essential
sections.p: Certain laboratory situations may give a false impression of normal MCV.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia with chest pain or syncope
Fever, weight loss, or lymphadenopathy suggesting marrow disease
